w2-opposite~idea.cta: Opposites and near-twins on the Word road
w2-opposite~idea.title: Opposites and near-twins
w2-opposite~idea.body: Words that mean the same, or nearly the same, are synonyms: big and large, start and begin. Words that mean the opposite are antonyms: hot and cold, full and empty. To check an opposite, put the two words in the same sentence — "The cup is full. The cup is empty." — and see if they pull in opposite directions. Watch out: a synonym can sneak in among the opposites.
w2-opposite~idea.more: I can find a word that means the same, or the opposite.

s2-tense~idea.cta: Past, present, future on the Sentence road
s2-tense~idea.title: Past, present, future
s2-tense~idea.body: The verb tells you WHEN. The past has already happened: Quill painted, Quill went. The present is happening now: Quill is painting. The future has not happened yet: Quill will paint. Many past verbs end in -ed, but some of the commonest do not: go → went, eat → ate, fly → flew. Time words like yesterday, now and tomorrow are clues.
s2-tense~idea.more: I can choose the verb that shows when something happens.

s2-tense~story.body: Yesterday Quill the fox painted the gate. Right now Quill is washing the brushes. Tomorrow Quill will paint the shed. "Same fox, same paint," says Quill, "but my verbs keep changing!"

s2-agree~idea.cta: Does it agree? on the Sentence road
s2-agree~idea.title: Does it agree?
s2-agree~idea.body: In standard written English the verb agrees with its subject. One fox runs; two foxes run. I am, you are, she is, they are. Find the subject first — the real one. In "The box of crayons is on the table", the subject is the box (one box), not the crayons. Two subjects joined by "and" make a plural: Quill and Bee are friends. (Some dialects do this differently, and that is not a mistake; here we practise the standard written form.)
s2-agree~idea.more: I can choose a verb that agrees with its subject.

s2-agree~story.cta: Does it agree? on the Sentence road
s2-agree~story.title: Does it agree?
s2-agree~story.body: Quill the fox wrote "The birds sings" and frowned. "One bird sings. Two birds sing," says Quill. "My verb has to match who is doing it."
